title: Audience requests and playing Sugar Blues
summary: He disliked copying others' material like Sugar Blues, preferring a straight Buck Clayton approach, and defends playing for the audience.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: yeah yeah I don't know what trumpet player was started it but I used to have to play sugar blues which I hated to do never liked to duplicate somebody else's material and I didn't feel a very strong affinity for it but we'd have to play things like that you mean with the mute
is that what you're talking about that type of sugar blues

yeah I don't think I didn't do that I played it I can remember hearing a very tasteful recording years ago by Buck Clayton Buck Clayton and Don Bias little quartet or quintet recording of sugar blues which they just played it very straightforward and honestly and I think that influenced me and I think I preferred to play it that way which of course would be a great disappointment to an audience that wanted to hear a lot of wah-wah rickety-tick razzmatazz things like things like Wabash Blues would come up well you know Ori would play the lead on that and do a little hokum that's fine you know audiences like that and after all you're playing for them I feel sorry for musicians who can only play for themselves it must be a fairly lonesome life
